title: Why Kochi Mini Cooper crash accused Suhail’s hairdo in custody caused a hullabaloo
content: Kochi: His long curls were part of his social-media persona. But when Suhail Sajeev, the 19-year-old prime accused in the Kochi Mini Cooper crash that killed three youths, appeared before the court with closely cropped hair, the dramatic makeover triggered a controversy of its own. Was it simply a haircut inside the Kakkanad Borstal School, where he is lodged as a remand prisoner, or could the change have implications for witness identification? The questions have put prison procedures, allegations of preferential treatment and the role of legal advisers under scrutiny. Suhail, accused of culpable homicide not amounting to murder in the fatal crash as he was allegedly drunk at the time of driving, had sported long, styled hair in photographs that circulated widely after the accident. The Instagram photos and videos of him posted by his mother too feature his long hair. His drastically altered appearance became public when he was brought out to the court while considering the custody application by the police, prompting allegations that the makeover could make identification by the witnesses more difficult. Besides Suhail, other accused persons also cut their hair in a similar manner. Police suspect possible legal advice Police sources said investigators suspect that the accused may have received legal advice regarding the change in appearance. They are examining the circumstances surrounding the haircut, including whether it could have been intended to complicate witness identification. We need to establish how the decision was taken and whether anyone advised or facilitated the change. Often lawyers advise their clients to trim hair and shave their beard prior to appearing before the court. Here, the haircut itself does not prove an attempt to mislead witnesses, but the circumstances surrounding it need to be examined, a police officer said, speaking on condition of anonymity. The allegation that the makeover was intended to derail a test identification parade has fuelled public criticism on social media. However, the motive remains unestablished. Police sources said that a change in hairstyle does not, by itself, prove an attempt to obstruct the investigation or establish that witness identification has been compromised. Trimmer, barber and Rule 477: Conflicting explanations The controversy deepened as questions emerged over how Suhail and the other accused were allowed to have their hair cropped while lodged at the Borstal School. Prisons Department sources initially maintained that Suhail had voluntarily used an electric trimmer available to inmates. A remand prisoner is not usually compelled to have his hair cut, except when a prison medical officer certifies in writing that close cropping is medically necessary. In this case, the accused youths volunteered to cut the hair themselves," a prison officer had told on Thursday when Suhail's new look became news. The officer also said electric trimmers were provided to them for personal grooming, without the need to bring in outside personnel. However, as criticism mounted, officials defended the practice as part of routine personal hygiene and refused to comment further. This is purely a matter of personal hygiene. The institution has a sanctioned capacity of 66 inmates, but more than 100 are currently accommodated here. Grooming is a routine process, and we cannot treat one inmate differently from the others or invite allegations of preferential treatment, a senior prison officer said, speaking on condition of anonymity. However, there are allegations that a barber had been brought into the facility on Wednesday morning to crop the hair of Suhail and the other accused. The conflicting reports have raised questions about who arranged the haircut and why...
